name: Gareth Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the maintenance foreman for the power company in our town, down by the river. Thirty-six years with the same firm, started as a trainee when I was twenty-two. A normal day, I'm in at seven, go through the work orders with my crew of five, and then we're out doing planned jobs: replacing an old pole, changing a transformer, or a day at one of the substations testing the switchgear. Afternoons I'm back at the depot signing off the jobs and arguing with the stores about parts.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's predictable. I know every substation in the district, I know which ones flood when the river's high and which ones the kids break into. What wears me out is change for the sake of it. Every new manager wants a new form. My wife Anita does all the online stuff at home, banking, booking the holidays, I wouldn't know where to start, and I'm happy with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. People get excited about every new thing and then it settles down. I wouldn't say much online, I'm not on any of it really. Maybe I'd mention it at the fishing club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to sixty-two, take my full pension and go fishing. I've got four years left and in this picture they're the same four years I was already planning. That's all I want, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep going to work, keep putting the extra into savings like we've done since the girls left home. Anita and I might look at doing the kitchen once I've retired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Calm. Like a normal Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has AI changed anything at your depot yet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. They gave the planners some new scheduling software and it put three jobs on the same truck on the same morning. We sorted it out with a phone call, like we always did. I've never used any of the AI things myself and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be planning for the next few years in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My retirement, mainly. The company pension is a good one, but the full amount only comes at sixty-two, when I've done forty years. I'll make sure I hit that date, then hand the crew over to Kev, who's ready for it.

S0.say: He'd say it's what he expected, since people get excited about every new thing and then it settles. He's not online, so he might just mention it at the fishing club.
S0.think: He thinks it means he reaches sixty-two, takes his full pension and goes fishing. The four years ahead stay the same four years he'd already planned.
S0.do: Keeps going to work and putting extra into savings as he has since his daughters left home. Plans to hit his full pension date at sixty-two, hand the crew to his deputy, and redo the kitchen afterwards.
S0.quote: I've got four years left and in this picture they're the same four years I was already planning.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth values predictability above all and has never used AI tools, leaving all online tasks to his wife. His life is organised around one date: full pension at sixty-two after forty years' service. He's pragmatic and unexcitable, and his idea of a problem solved is a phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll cope, we always have. When they brought in the computers in the nineties people said the same thing. At work I'd tell the lads to keep their heads down and do the job well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd want it to wait four years. I'm not against it, I just don't want to be learning new tricks in my last stretch. If they want me looking at a screen, they can wait till I've handed in my keys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they told me to do and not a minute more. I'd let Kev take the lead on anything new, since he'll be foreman after me anyway. I'd keep saving the same as now and stick to my date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit irritated, but not worried. It's a nuisance, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the new tools if they came in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had to, I'd learn the basics. I'd be slow, and I'd probably get Kev or Anita to help me. But I'd rather do it the way I know, and in most of the jobs we do, a pole is still a pole and a bolt is still a bolt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would this affect most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young lads who do the inspections and the meter checks, maybe. If a drone and a computer can do the patrols, there's less of that kind of work. But there are plenty of jobs at the other power companies and the contractors round here, so they'd find something.

S1.say: He'd say they'll cope, as they did when computers came in during the nineties. He'd tell his crew to keep their heads down and do the job well.
S1.think: He'd privately want it to wait four years so he isn't learning new tricks in his last stretch. He's not against it, he just wants to have handed in his keys first.
S1.do: Does the training required and no more, letting his deputy take the lead on new tools. Keeps saving at the same rate and sticks to his planned retirement date.
S1.feel: A bit irritated but not worried; it's a nuisance, not a threat.
S1.quote: If they want me looking at a screen, they can wait till I've handed in my keys.
S1.fieldNote: He sees steady change as an annoyance rather than a danger, mostly because he's so close to retirement and there are plenty of local jobs for younger staff. He'd hand anything new to his successor. His comparison to the nineties computers shows he's seen change before and outlasted it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's madness and nobody's ready. At work I'd tell people not to panic and wait for the company to say something. With friends I'd say the government had better have a plan, though I doubt they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one bothers me. Two years puts me at sixty, two years short of my forty years. If they let me go at sixty, I lose about a tenth of my pension for the rest of my life, and that's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd ask the pension office for the numbers if I went early. I'd cut back on the kitchen plans and the holiday, and put more into savings while I still had the wage. If the company offered a decent package, I'd take it rather than fight, but I'd wait to see what they put on the table first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared for the roof over our heads, but annoyed and worried that the plan I've had for years gets broken at the last bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've mentioned the pension at sixty-two a lot. What happens to it here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a final-salary scheme, so every year counts. We'd manage on the smaller one, the house is nearly paid off and we've got savings. But I've earned that full pension and I'd be angry to lose it because of a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning the new systems to stay on those two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'd be fighting something I don't understand, at sixty, against people half my age who grew up with it. I'd rather take what they offer and go. Anita would probably tell me I'm being stubborn, and she'd be right.

S2.say: He'd call it madness that nobody is ready, tell colleagues not to panic and wait for the company to say something. With friends he'd say the government had better have a plan, though he doubts it.
S2.think: This picture bothers him: it puts him at sixty, two years short of forty years' service. Going early would cost him about a tenth of his pension for life.
S2.do: Asks the pension office for early-leaving figures and cuts back the kitchen and holiday plans while saving more of his wage. Waits to see what package the company offers and would take a decent one rather than fight or retrain.
S2.feel: Anxious: not scared for his home, but worried and annoyed that his long-held plan breaks at the very end.
S2.quote: If they let me go at sixty, I lose about a tenth of my pension for the rest of my life, and that's not nothing.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits the one thing he cares about, the full pension date. He's not frightened about money, but he's angry at losing what he's earned. He admits refusing to learn the new systems is stubbornness, and accepts it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to get ready, so let's see what the company does. I'd tell the lads it's coming but not to throw their toolbags in the river. I'd not say anything online, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly be safe, since I'd have my forty years by then. What worries me is the run-up, when the company starts trimming staff to get ready. They always cut the expensive old ones first, and I'm the most expensive old one on the books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and make myself hard to get rid of, doing the jobs nobody else knows, like the old substations. I'd put a bit more aside in case they push me out at sixty-one. Otherwise I'd keep going till my date and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's further off, but there's still a gap where it could catch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-three in 2031. Does that mean you're safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly, yes. If I get to sixty-two, I'm fine, whatever happens after. The danger is a restructuring at sixty-one, which is when companies like to tidy up before something big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with the warning time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down everything I know about the old substations, which ones flood, which relays are temperamental. Not for the robots, for Kev. That way they need me to explain it, and he's got it when I'm gone.

S3.say: He'd say there's time to get ready and wait to see what the company does, telling his crew not to give up on the trade. He'd say nothing online as usual.
S3.think: He thinks he'd mostly be safe with his forty years done by 2031. His worry is a pre-arrival restructuring that cuts expensive older staff like him at sixty-one.
S3.do: Keeps his head down and makes himself hard to replace by handling the old substations nobody else knows. Saves a bit extra in case he's pushed out at sixty-one, and writes down his substation knowledge for his deputy.
S3.feel: Uneasy: it's further off, but there's still a gap where it could catch him.
S3.quote: They always cut the expensive old ones first, and I'm the most expensive old one on the books.
S3.fieldNote: His worry here is specific and practical: companies trim expensive older staff before a big change. His plan is to make himself indispensable through old knowledge rather than new skills. Writing it down for his successor is a quiet act of loyalty to the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so I wouldn't make a fuss. I'd tell the young lads to learn the new stuff while they've got time. Same as always, no posting online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's nothing. By 2036 I'll be on the riverbank with a flask, and the robots can argue with the stores about parts. I'll be well out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly what I'd do anyway. Work to sixty-two, take the full pension, hand over to Kev, do the kitchen. Maybe help the girls a bit if they need it later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit sorry for the young ones, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your daughters, who'd be in mid-career by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shreya's an accountant, and I hear that's the kind of job these things go after first. Meera lives overseas and teaches music, so maybe she's all right. I'd tell them both to save hard while they're earning, same as I did, because nobody else will look after you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change, knowing it was coming in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Maybe I'd put a bit more aside for the girls. But I'm not going to change the habits of a lifetime for something ten years off that might not happen the way they say.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so he wouldn't fuss. He'd tell younger colleagues to learn the new systems while they have time.
S4.think: He thinks it means nothing for him, since by 2036 he'll be retired and fishing. He'd be well out of it.
S4.do: Works to sixty-two, takes his full pension, hands over to his deputy and redoes the kitchen as planned. Puts a little more aside to help his daughters later if needed.
S4.feel: Calm, a bit sorry for the young ones.
S4.quote: I'd tell them both to save hard while they're earning, same as I did, because nobody else will look after you.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, his whole worry disappears because his pension date comes first. He thinks of his daughters but his advice is self-reliance, not policy. He openly doubts it will happen the way people say, which fits his steady scepticism.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it catches me just short of my full pension. What would help is if anyone over fifty-five who lost their job because of these machines got their pension counted as if they'd done the full years. That's all I'd ask. I'm not after a handout, just what I'd have earned.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe ask about the river. When it floods, half the substations go under, and no computer is going to wade in there. Somebody who knows where the drains are still has to.

headlineQuote: By 2036 I'll be on the riverbank with a flask, and the robots can argue with the stores about parts.
portrait: Gareth Patel is a 58-year-old maintenance foreman who has spent thirty-six years with the same power company in a river town, and he knows every substation that floods. He has never used AI, leaves all online tasks to his wife, and organises his life around one date: full pension at sixty-two after forty years. In the plateau and steady change pictures he's calm or mildly irritated, happy to let his deputy take on new tools. The two-year AGI picture makes him anxious because it could cost him a tenth of his pension, while the longer pictures leave him safely retired, with only a small worry about a restructuring in the run-up.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture worries him most, because it would catch him two years short of his full pension.
whatWouldHelp: Pension counted as if the full years were worked for anyone over fifty-five who loses their job to the machines; not a handout, just what he'd have earned.
